entries.48150625345ab48e0c802d34d33ba60faa5686c7: <div sID="gen10869" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="29" osisID="Ps.29" sID="Ps.29"/> <div eID="gen10869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10870" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10871" type="x-p"/> It is the probable conjecture of some very good interpreters that David penned this psalm upon occasion, and just at the time, of a great storm of thunder, lightning, and rain, as the eighth psalm was his meditation in a moon-light night and the nineteenth in a sunny morning. It is good to take occasion from the sensible operations of God's power in the kingdom of nature to give glory to him. So composed was David, and so cheerful, even in a dreadful tempest, when others trembled, that then he penned this psalm; for, "though the earth be removed, yet will we not fear." I. He calls upon the great ones of the world to give glory to God, <reference osisRef="Ps.29.1-Ps.29.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. II. To convince them of the goodness of that God whom they were to adore, he takes notice of his power and terror in the thunder, and lightning, and thunder-showers (<reference osisRef="Ps.29.3-Ps.29.9">ver. 3-9</reference>), his sovereign dominion over the world (<reference osisRef="Ps.29.10">ver. 10</reference>), and his special favour to his church, <reference osisRef="Ps.29.11">ver. 11</reference>. Great and high thoughts of God should fill us in singing this psalm.
entries.81610dba3f1216d33d3acde10676af60ec0b85d9: <div eID="gen10871" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10870" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Glory of the Lord.</title> <div sID="gen10872" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Give unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , O ye mighty, give unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> glory and strength. <hi type="super">2</hi> Give unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> the glory due unto his name; worship the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> in the beauty of holiness. <hi type="super">3</hi> The voice of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> upon the waters: the God of glory thundereth: the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> upon many waters. <hi type="super">4</hi> The voice of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> powerful; the voice of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> full of majesty. <hi type="super">5</hi> The voice of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> breaketh the cedars; yea, the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> breaketh the cedars of Lebanon. <hi type="super">6</hi> He maketh them also to skip like a calf; Lebanon and Sirion like a young unicorn. <hi type="super">7</hi> The voice of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> divideth the flames of fire. <hi type="super">8</hi> The voice of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shaketh the wilderness; the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shaketh the wilderness of Kadesh. <hi type="super">9</hi> The voice of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> maketh the hinds to calve, and discovereth the forests: and in his temple doth every one speak of <hi type="italic">his</hi> glory. <hi type="super">10</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> sitteth upon the flood; yea, the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> sitteth King for ever. <hi type="super">11</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> will give strength unto his people; the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> will bless his people with peace. <div eID="gen10872" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10873" type="x-p"/> In this psalm we have, <div eID="gen10873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10874" type="x-p"/> I. A demand of the homage of the great men of the earth to be paid to the great God. Every clap of thunder David interpreted as a call to himself and other princes to give glory to the great God. Observe, 1. Who they are that are called to this duty: <hi type="italic">"O you mighty</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.29.1">v. 1</reference>), you sons of the mighty, who have power, and on whom that power is devolved by succession and inheritance, who have royal blood running in your veins!" It is much for the honour of the great God that the men of this world should pay their homage to him; and they are bound to do it, not only because, high as they are, he is infinitely above them, and therefore they must bow to him, but because they have their power from him, and are to use it for him, and this tribute of acknowledgment they owe to him for it. 2. How often this call is repeated; <hi type="italic">Give unto the Lord,</hi> and again, and a third time, <hi type="italic">Give unto the Lord.</hi> This intimates that the mighty men are backward to this duty and are with difficulty persuaded to it, but that it is of great consequence to the interests of God's kingdom among men that princes should heartily espouse them. Jerusalem flourishes when the <hi type="italic">kings of the earth bring their glory and honour into it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.21.24">Rev. xxi. 24</reference>. 3. What they are called to do—to <hi type="italic">give unto the Lord,</hi> not as if he needed any thing, or could be benefited by any gifts of ours, nor as if we had any thing to give him that is not his own already (<hi type="italic">Who hath first given to him?</hi>), but the recognition of his glory, and of his dominion over us, he is pleased to interpret as a gift to him: "<hi type="italic">Give unto the Lord</hi> your own selves, in the first place, and then your services. <hi type="italic">Give unto the Lord glory and strength;</hi> acknowledge his glory and strength, and give praise to him as a God of infinite majesty and irresistible power; and whatever glory or strength he has by his providence entrusted you with offer it to him, to be used for his honour, in his service. Give him your crowns; let them be laid at his feet; give him your sceptres, your swords, your keys, put all into his hand, that you, in the use of them, may be to him for a name and a praise." Princes value themselves by their glory and strength; these they must ascribe to God, owning him to be infinitely more glorious and powerful than they. This demand of homage from the mighty must be looked upon as directed either to the grandees of David's own kingdom, the peers of the realm, the princes of the tribes (and it is to excite them to a more diligent and constant attendance at God's altars, in which he had observed them very remiss), or to the neighbouring kings whom he by his sword had made tributaries to Israel and now would persuade to become tributaries to the God of Israel. Crowned heads must bow before the King of kings. What is here said to the mighty is said to all: <hi type="italic">Worship God;</hi> it is the sum and substance of the everlasting gospel, <reference osisRef="Rev.14.6-Rev.14.7">Rev. xiv. 6, 7</reference>. Now we have here, (1.) The nature of religious worship; it is <hi type="italic">giving to the Lord the glory due to his name,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.29.2">v. 2</reference>. God's name is that whereby he has made himself known. There is a glory due to his name. It is impossible that we should give him all the glory due to his name; when we have said and done our best for the honour of God's name, still we come infinitely short of the merit of the subject; but when we answer that revelation which he has made of himself, with suitable affections and adorations, then we give him some of that glory which is due to his name. If we would, in hearing and praying, and other acts of devotion, receive grace from God, we must make it our business to give glory to God. (2.) The rule of the performance of religious exercises; <hi type="italic">Worship the Lord in the beauty of holiness,</hi> which denotes, [1.] The object of our worship; the glorious majesty of God is called <hi type="italic">the beauty of holiness,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.21">2 Chron. xx. 21</reference>. In the worship of God we must have an eye to his beauty, and adore him, not only as infinitely awful and therefore to be feared above all, but as infinitely amiable and therefore to be loved and delighted in above all; especially we must have an eye to the beauty of his holiness; this the angels fasten upon in their praises, <reference osisRef="Rev.4.8">Rev. iv. 8</reference>. Or, [2.] The place of worship. The sanctuary then was the <hi type="italic">beauty of holiness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.48.1-Ps.48.2">Ps. xlviii. 1, 2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.17.12">Jer. xvii. 12</reference>. The beauty of the sanctuary was the exact agreement of the worship there performed with the divine appointment—the pattern in the mount. Now, under the gospel, solemn assemblies of Christians (which purity is the beauty of) are the places where God is to be worshipped. Or, [3.] The manner of worship. We must be holy in all our religious performances, devoted to God, and to his will and glory. There is a beauty in holiness, and it is that which puts an acceptable beauty upon all the acts of worship. <div eID="gen10874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10875" type="x-p"/> II. Good reason given for this demand. We shall see ourselves bound to give glory to God if we consider, <div eID="gen10875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10876" type="x-p"/> 1. His sufficiency in himself, intimated in his name <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi>—<hi type="italic">I am that I am,</hi> which is repeated here no fewer than eighteen times in this short psalm, twice in every verse but three, and once in two of those three; I do not recollect that there is the like in all the book of psalms. Let the mighty ones of the earth know him by this name and give him the glory due to it. <div eID="gen10876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10877" type="x-p"/> 2. His sovereignty over all things. Let those that rule over men know there is a God that rules over them, that rules over all. The psalmist here sets forth God's dominion, <div eID="gen10877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10878" type="x-p"/> (1.) In the kingdom of nature. In the wonderful effects of natural causes, and the operations of the powers of nature, we ought to take notice of God's glory and strength, which we are called upon to ascribe to him; in the thunder, and lightning, and rain, we may see, [1.] His glory. It is the God of glory that thunders (thunders is the <hi type="italic">noise of his voice,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.37.2">Job xxxvii. 2</reference>), and it declares him a God of glory, so awful is the sound of the thunder, and so bright the flash of its companion, the lightning; to the hearing and to the sight nothing is more affecting than these, as if by those two learning senses God would have such proofs of his glory to the minds of men as should leave the most stupid inexcusable. Some observe that there were then some particular reasons why thunder should be called <hi type="italic">the voice of the Lord,</hi> not only because it comes from above, is not under the direction or foresight of any man, speaks aloud, and reaches far, but because God often spoke in thunder, particularly at Mount Sinai, and by thunder discomfited the enemies of Israel. To speak it the voice of the God of glory, it is here said to be <hi type="italic">upon the water,</hi> upon <hi type="italic">many waters</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.29.3">v. 3</reference>); it reaches over the vast ocean, the waters under the firmament; it rattles among the thick clouds, the waters above the firmament. Every one that hears the thunder (his ear being made to tingle with it) will own that <hi type="italic">the voice of the Lord is full of majesty</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.29.4">Ps. xxix. 4</reference>), enough to make the highest humble (for none can <hi type="italic">thunder with a voice like him</hi>) and the proudest tremble—for, if his voice be so terrible, what is his arm? Every time we hear it thunder, let our hearts be thereby filled with great, and high, and honourable thoughts of God, in the holy adorings and admirings of whom the power of godliness does so much consist. <hi type="italic">O Lord our God! thou art very great.</hi> [2.] His power (<reference osisRef="Ps.29.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">The voice of the Lord is powerful,</hi> as appears by the effects of it; for it works wonders. Those that write natural histories relate the prodigious effects of thunder and lightning, even out of the ordinary course of natural causes, which must be resolved into the omnipotence of the God of nature. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Trees have been rent and split by thunderbolts, <reference osisRef="Ps.29.5-Ps.29.6">v. 5, 6</reference>. <hi type="italic">The voice of the Lord,</hi> in the thunder, often <hi type="italic">broke the cedars,</hi> even those of Lebanon, the strongest, the stateliest. Some understand it of the violent winds which shook the cedars, and sometimes tore off their aspiring tops. Earthquakes also shook the ground itself on which the trees grew, and made <hi type="italic">Lebanon and Sirion</hi> to dance; <hi type="italic">the wilderness of Kadesh</hi> also was in like manner shaken (<reference osisRef="Ps.29.8">v. 8</reference>), the trees by winds, the ground by earthquakes, and both by thunders, of which I incline rather to understand it. The learned Dr. Hammond understands it of the consternations and conquest of neighbouring kingdoms that warred with Israel and opposed David, as the Syrians, whose country lay near the forest of Lebanon, the Amorites that bordered on Mount Hermon, and the Moabites and Ammonites that lay about the wilderness of Kadesh. <hi type="italic">Secondly.</hi> Fires have been kindled by lightnings and houses and churches thereby consumed; hence we read of hot thunderbolts (<reference osisRef="Ps.78.48">Ps. lxxviii. 48</reference>); accordingly the voice of the Lord, in the thunder, is here said to <hi type="italic">divide the flames of fire</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.29.7">v. 7</reference>), that is, to scatter them upon the earth, as God sees fit to direct them and do execution by them. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> The terror of thunder makes the hinds to calve sooner, and some think more easily, than otherwise they would. The hind is a timourous creature, and much affected with the noise of thunder; and no marvel, when sometimes proud and stout men have been made to tremble at it. The emperor Caligula would hide himself under his bed when it thundered. Horace, the poet, owns that he was reclaimed from atheism by the terror of thunder and lightning, which he describes somewhat like this of David, <hi type="italic">lib.</hi> 1, <hi type="italic">ode</hi> 34. The thunder is said here to <hi type="italic">discover the forest,</hi> that is, it so terrifies the wild beasts of the forest that they quit the dens and thickets in which they hid themselves are so are discovered. Or it throws down the trees, and so discovers the ground that was shaded by them. Whenever it thunders let us think of this psalm; and, whenever we sing this psalm, let us think of the dreadful thunder-claps we have sometimes heard, and thus bring God's words and his works together, that by both we may be directed and quickened to give unto him the glory due unto his name; and let us bless him that there is another voice of his besides this dreadful one, by which God now speaks to us, even the still small voice of his gospel, the terror of which shall not make us afraid. <div eID="gen10878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10879" type="x-p"/> (2.) In the kingdom of providence, <reference osisRef="Ps.29.10">v. 10</reference>. God is to be praised as the governor of the world of mankind. He <hi type="italic">sits upon the flood; he sits King for ever.</hi> He not only sits at rest in the enjoyment of himself, but he sits as King in the throne which he has <hi type="italic">prepared in the heavens</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.103.19">Ps. ciii. 19</reference>), where he takes cognizance of, and gives orders about, all the affairs of the children of men, and does all according to his will, according to the counsel of his will. Observe, [1.] The power of his kingdom: He <hi type="italic">sits upon the flood.</hi> As he has founded the earth, so he has founded his own throne, upon the floods, <reference osisRef="Ps.24.2">Ps. xxiv. 2</reference>. The ebbings and flowings of this lower world, and the agitations and revolutions of the affairs in it, give not the least shake to the repose nor to the counsels of the Eternal Mind. The opposition of his enemies is compared to the flood (<reference osisRef="Ps.93.3-Ps.93.4">Ps. xciii. 3, 4</reference>); but the Lord sits upon it; he crushes it, conquers it, and completes his own purposes in despite of all the devices that are in men's hearts. The word here translated <hi type="italic">the flood</hi> is never used but concerning Noah's flood; and therefore some think it is that which is here spoken of. God did sit upon that flood as a Judge executing the sentence of his justice upon the world of the ungodly that was swept away by it. And he still sits upon the flood, restraining the waters of Noah, that they turn not again to cover the earth, according to his promise never to <hi type="italic">destroy the earth any more by a flood,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.9.11">Gen. ix. 11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.54.9">Isa. liv. 9</reference>. [2.] The perpetuity of his kingdom; <hi type="italic">He sits King for ever;</hi> no period can, or shall, be put to his government. The administration of his kingdom is consonant to his counsels from eternity and pursuant to his designs for eternity. <div eID="gen10879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10880" type="x-p"/> (3.) In the kingdom of grace. Here his glory shines most brightly, [1.] In the adorations he receives from the subjects of that kingdom (<reference osisRef="Ps.29.9">v. 9</reference>). <hi type="italic">In his temple,</hi> where people attend his discoveries of himself and his mind and attend him with their praises, <hi type="italic">every one speaks of his glory.</hi> In the world every man sees it, or at least <hi type="italic">may behold it afar off</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.36.25">Job xxxvi. 25</reference>); but it is only in the temple, in the church, that it is spoken of to his honour. <hi type="italic">All his works do praise him</hi> (that is, they minister matter for praise), but his saints only do bless him, and speak of his glory of his works, <reference osisRef="Ps.145.10">Ps. cxlv. 10</reference>. [2.] In the favours he bestows upon the subjects of that kingdom, <reference osisRef="Ps.29.11">v. 11</reference>. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> He will qualify them for his service: <hi type="italic">He will give strength to his people,</hi> to fortify them against every evil work and to furnish them for every good work; out of weakness they shall be made strong; nay, he will perfect strength in weakness. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> He will encourage them in his service: <hi type="italic">He will bless his people with peace.</hi> Peace is a blessing of inestimable value, which God designs for all his people. The <hi type="italic">work of righteousness is peace (great peace have those that love thy law</hi>); but much more the crown of righteousness: the end of righteousness is peace; it is endless peace. When the thunder of God's wrath shall make sinners tremble the saints shall lift up their heads with joy.  <chapter eID="Ps.29"/> <div eID="gen10880" type="x-p"/>

entries.1b8422c21840d942ea8ebe41e3d9b6e2cbc565a7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5763"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 29</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.29.1-Ps.29.11">Psa 29:1-11</reference>. Trust in God is encouraged by the celebration of His mighty power as illustrated in His dominion over the natural world, in some of its most terrible and wonderful exhibitions.</title> <div sID="gen8774" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5763"/><hi type="bold">1. Give--</hi>or, "ascribe" (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.3">De 32:3</reference>).<div eID="gen8774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8775" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mighty--</hi>or, "sons of the mighty" (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.6">Psa 89:6</reference>). Heavenly beings, as angels. <div eID="gen8775" type="x-p"/>
entries.4af412e2359a234117452c37a3d9c560de4ad3eb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5764"/><div sID="gen8776" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5764"/><hi type="bold">2. name--</hi>as (<reference osisRef="Ps.5.11">Psa 5:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.8.1">8:1</reference>).<div eID="gen8776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8777" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">beauty of holiness--</hi>the loveliness of a spiritual worship, of which the perceptible beauty of the sanctuary worship was but a type. <div eID="gen8777" type="x-p"/>
entries.291173393fb5034f0117e71da9bdb24abfdbf3d9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5765"/><div sID="gen8778" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5765"/><hi type="bold">3. The voice of the Lord--</hi>audible exhibition of His power in the tempest, of which thunder is a specimen, but not the uniform or sole example.<div eID="gen8778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8779" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the waters--</hi>the clouds or vapors (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.11">Psa 18:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.10.13">Jr 10:13</reference>). <div eID="gen8779" type="x-p"/>
entries.3296cfa52935cc858fbef7de2d50e5a7442dd004: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5766"/><div sID="gen8780" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5766"/><hi type="bold">4. powerful ... majesty--</hi>literally, "in power, in majesty." <div eID="gen8780" type="x-p"/>
entries.31255d7ecdb714b54d6a7018f548ab835d7f8c0a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5767"/><div sID="gen8781" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5767"/>5-6. The tall and large cedars, especially of Lebanon, are shivered, utterly broken. The waving of the mountain forests before the wind is expressed by the figure of skipping or leaping. <div eID="gen8781" type="x-p"/>
entries.1f9131a20d2b12159551e850b13919331da910bc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5768"/><div sID="gen8782" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5768"/><hi type="bold">7. divideth--</hi>literally, "hews off." The lightning, like flakes and splinters hewed from stone or wood, flies through the air. <div eID="gen8782" type="x-p"/>
entries.d9011418fb254b0a91bb9eda3ed6e13cb9d716ef: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5769"/><div sID="gen8783" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5769"/><hi type="bold">8. the wilderness--</hi>especially Kadesh, south of Judea, is selected as another scene of this display of divine power, as a vast and desolate region impresses the mind, like mountains, with images of grandeur. <div eID="gen8783" type="x-p"/>
entries.3b5d020261d299a52a4885e0e2b1953b884afeff: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5770"/><div sID="gen8784" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5770"/>9. Terror-stricken animals and denuded forests close the illustration. In view of this scene of awful sublimity, God's worshippers respond to the call of <reference osisRef="Ps.29.2">Psa 29:2</reference>, and speak or cry, "Glory!" By "temple," or "palace" (God's residence, <reference osisRef="Ps.5.7">Psa 5:7</reference>), may here be meant heaven, or the whole frame of nature, as the angels are called on for praise. <div eID="gen8784" type="x-p"/>
entries.f095f7624e28d4ec69decac215e1b92dd142e98e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5771"/><div sID="gen8785" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5771"/>10-11. Over this terrible raging of the elements God is enthroned, directing and restraining by sovereign power; and hence the comfort of His people. "This awful God is ours, our Father and our Love." <chapter eID="Ps.29"/>

entries.83d6adf99a638e2770641a75e3c8b48ec45fd0c7: <div eID="gen19441" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen19442" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19443" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19443" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19442" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19444" type="x-p"/> The psalmist calls upon the great and mighty to give thanks unto God, and to worship him in the beauty of holiness, on account of a tempest that had taken place, <reference osisRef="Psa.29.1">Psa 29:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.29.2">Psa 29:2</reference>. He shouts the wonders produced by a thunderstorm, which he calls the voice of God, <reference osisRef="Psa.29.3-Psa.29.9">Psa 29:3-9</reference>. Speaks of the majesty of God, <reference osisRef="Psa.29.10">Psa 29:10</reference>; and points out the good he will do to his people, <reference osisRef="Psa.29.11">Psa 29:11</reference>. <div eID="gen19444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19445" type="x-p"/> In the Hebrew, this is called A Psalm for David. The Vulgate says, "A Psalm of David, when the tabernacle was completed." The Septuagint says: "A Psalm of David, at the going out or exodus of the tabernacle." The Arabic states it to be "A prophecy concerning the incarnation; and concerning the ark and the tent." <reference osisRef="Num.5.12">Num 5:12</reference>. The Syriac, "A Psalm of David, concerning oblation." The Psalm was probably written to commemorate the abundant rain which fell in the days of David, after the heavens had been shut up for three years; <reference osisRef="2Sam.21.1-2Sam.21.10">2Sam 21:1-10</reference>. <div eID="gen19445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19446" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen19446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19447" type="x-p"/> O ye mighty - בני אלים beney elim, "sons of the strong ones," or "sons of rams." The Chaldee has, "Ye hosts of angels, sons of God." The Vulgate has, "Offer to the Lord, ye sons of God; offer to the Lord the sons of rams;" in this rendering agree the Septuagint, Ethiopic Arabic, and Anglo-Saxon. The old Psalter has, Bringes til Lord ye goddes sonnes; brynges til Lord sonnes of wether: which it paraphrases thus: that es, yourself, sonnes of apostles, that war leders of goddes folk; qwam ye study to folow. <div eID="gen19447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19448" type="x-p"/> Glory and strength - Ascribe all excellence and might to him. <div eID="gen19448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19449" type="x-p"/> The whole Psalm is employed in describing the effects produced by a thunder-storm which had lately taken place.
entries.488704b4124e3a2375e5681e7fd4fa23d659e649: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen19449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19450" type="x-p"/> The glory due unto his name - Rather, the glory of his name. His name is Mercy; his nature is love. Ascribe mercy, love, power, and wisdom to him. All these are implied in the name Jehovah. <div eID="gen19450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19451" type="x-p"/> In the beauty of holiness - בהדרת קדש behadrath kodesh, "the beautiful garments of holiness." Let the priests and Levites put on their best and cleanest apparel; and let the whole service be conducted in such a way as to be no dishonor to the Divine Majesty. The Vulgate and others read, In the palace of his holiness. Let all go to the temple, and return thanks to God for their preservation during this dreadful storm. See on <reference osisRef="Psa.29.9">Psa 29:9</reference> (note).
entries.393eee54af6f15039db2abc265245dcf11948fe0: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen19451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19452" type="x-p"/> The voice of the Lord - Thunder, so called, <reference osisRef="Exo.9.23">Exo 9:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.9.28">Exo 9:28</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.9.29">Exo 9:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.37.4">Job 37:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Psa.18.13">Psa 18:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.30.30">Isa 30:30</reference>. On this subject see the note on <reference osisRef="Job.37.4">Job 37:4</reference>, where there is a particular description of the nature and generation of thunder; and of the lightning, clap, rain, and other phenomena which accompany it. <div eID="gen19452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19453" type="x-p"/> Upon many waters - The clouds, which Moses calls the waters which are above the firmament.
entries.5e3afb5399fc0aeb52676529b360bcc8fb442d54: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen19453" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19454" type="x-p"/> Is powerful - There is no agent in universal nature so powerful as the electric fluid. It destroys life, tears castles and towers to pieces, rends the strongest oaks, and cleaves the most solid rocks: universal animate nature is awed and terrified by it. To several of these effects the psalmist here refers; and for the illustration of the whole I must refer to the above notes on Job. <div eID="gen19454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19455" type="x-p"/> Full of majesty - No sound in nature is so tremendous and majestic as that of thunder; it is the most fit to represent the voice of God.
entries.69d17ba9361b1570ef2c66f48fd60142ce5d387b: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen19455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19456" type="x-p"/> Breaketh the cedars - Very tall trees attract the lightning from the clouds, by which they are often torn to pieces. Woods and forests give dreadful proof of this after a thunderstorm.
entries.d47ca5a06a16a3a3e5f8c3ca725bc253a860078e: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen19456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19457" type="x-p"/> Divideth the flames of fire - The forked zigzag lightning is the cause of thunder; and in a thunder-storm these liahtnings are variously dispersed, smiting houses, towers, trees, men, and cattle, in different places.
entries.bb97ea43cfac586ac6336145bca2845ff2b33138: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen19457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19458" type="x-p"/> The wilderness of Kadesh - This was on the frontiers of Idumea and Paran. There may be a reference to some terrible thunder-storm and earthquake which had occurred in that place.
entries.9d34a2937ebfabbe51c619c3fa7ea0975fe2c0fe: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen19458" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19459" type="x-p"/> Maketh the hinds to calve - Strikes terror through all the tribes of animals; which sometimes occasions those which are pregnant to cast their young. This, I believe, to be the whole that is meant by the text. I meddle not with the fables which have been published on this subject both by ancients and moderns. <div eID="gen19459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19460" type="x-p"/> Discovereth the forests - Makes them sometimes evident in the darliest night, by the sudden flash; and often by setting them on fire. <div eID="gen19460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19461" type="x-p"/> And in his temple - Does this refer to the effect which a dreadful thunder-storm often produces? Multitudes run to places of worship as asylums in order to find safety, and pray to God. See on <reference osisRef="Psa.29.2">Psa 29:2</reference> (note).
entries.10a33f76a0ea6907501a3daba48378d908e830aa: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen19461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19462" type="x-p"/> The Lord sitteth upon the flood - יהוה למבול ישב Jehovah lammabbul yasheb, "Jehovah sat upon the deluge." It was Jehovah that commanded those waters to be upon the earth. He directed the storm; and is here represented, after all the confusion and tempest, as sitting on the floods, appeasing the fury of the jarring elements; and reducing all things, by his governing influence, to regularity and order. <div eID="gen19462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19463" type="x-p"/> Sitteth king for ever - He governs universal nature; whatsoever he wills he does, in the heavens above, in the earth beneath, and in all deep places. Every phenomenon is under his government and control. There is something very like this in Virgil's description of Neptune appeasing the storm raised by Juno for the destruction of the fleet of Aeneas. See at the end of this Psalm.
entries.aed4b13bd2ee797fe7473bc1e614e0c19a8aa23f: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen19463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19464" type="x-p"/> The Lord will give strength - Prosperity in our secular affairs; success in our enterprises; and his blessing upon our fields and cattle. <div eID="gen19464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19465" type="x-p"/> The Lord will bless his people with peace - Give them victory over their enemies, and cause the nations to be at peace with them; so that they shall enjoy uninterrupted prosperity. The plentiful rain which God has now sent is a foretaste of his future blessings and abundant mercies. <div eID="gen19465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19466" type="x-p"/> In the note on <reference osisRef="Psa.29.10">Psa 29:10</reference> I have referred to the following description taken from Virgil. Did he borrow some of the chief ideas in it from the 29th Psalm? The reader will observe several coincidences. <div eID="gen19466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19467" type="x-p"/> Interea magno misceri murmure pontum, <div eID="gen19467" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19468" type="x-p"/> Emissamque hyemem sensit Neptunus, et imis <div eID="gen19468" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19469" type="x-p"/> Stagna refusa vadis: graviter commotus, et alto <div eID="gen19469" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19470" type="x-p"/> Prospiciens, summa placidum caput extulit unda. <div eID="gen19470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19471" type="x-p"/> Disjectam Aeneae toto videt aequore classem, <div eID="gen19471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19472" type="x-p"/> Fluctibus oppressos Troas, coelique ruina. <div eID="gen19472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19473" type="x-p"/> Eurum ad se zephyrumque vocat: dehinc talia fatur <div eID="gen19473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19474" type="x-p"/> Sic ait: et dicto citius tumida aequora placat, <div eID="gen19474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19475" type="x-p"/> Collectasque fugat nubes, solemque reducit. <div eID="gen19475" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19476" type="x-p"/> Cymothoe simul, et Triton adnixus acuto <div eID="gen19476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19477" type="x-p"/> Detrudunt naves scopulo; levat ipse tridenti; <div eID="gen19477" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19478" type="x-p"/> Et vastas aperit syrtes, et temperat aequor, <div eID="gen19478" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19479" type="x-p"/> Atque rotis summas levibus perlabitur undas. <div eID="gen19479" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19480" type="x-p"/> Sic cunctus pelagi cecidit fragor, aequora postquam <div eID="gen19480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19481" type="x-p"/> Prospiciens genitor, caeloque invectus aperto, <div eID="gen19481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19482" type="x-p"/> Flectit equos, curruque volans dat lora secundo. <div eID="gen19482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19483" type="x-p"/> Aen. lib. i., ver. 124. "Mean time, imperial Neptune heard the sound <div eID="gen19483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19484" type="x-p"/> Of raging billows breaking on the ground. <div eID="gen19484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19485" type="x-p"/> Displeased, and fearing for his watery reign, <div eID="gen19485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19486" type="x-p"/> He rears his awful head above the main, <div eID="gen19486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19487" type="x-p"/> Serene in majesty; then rolled his eyes <div eID="gen19487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19488" type="x-p"/> Around the space of earth, of seas, and skies. <div eID="gen19488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19489" type="x-p"/> He saw the Trojan fleet dispersed, distressed, <div eID="gen19489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19490" type="x-p"/> By stormy winds and wintry heaven oppressed. <div eID="gen19490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19491" type="x-p"/> He summoned Eurus and the Western Blast, <div eID="gen19491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19492" type="x-p"/> And first an angry glance on both he cast; <div eID="gen19492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19493" type="x-p"/> Then thus rebuked. <div eID="gen19493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19494" type="x-p"/> He spoke; and while he spoke, he soothed the sea, <div eID="gen19494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19495" type="x-p"/> Dispelled the darkness, and restored the day. <div eID="gen19495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19496" type="x-p"/> Cymothoe, Triton, and the sea-green train <div eID="gen19496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19497" type="x-p"/> Of beauteous nymphs, and daughters of the main, <div eID="gen19497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19498" type="x-p"/> Clear from the rocks the vessels with their hands; <div eID="gen19498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19499" type="x-p"/> The god himself with ready trident stands, <div eID="gen19499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19500" type="x-p"/> And opes the deep, and spreads the moving sands; <div eID="gen19500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19501" type="x-p"/> Then heaves them off the shoals: where'er he guides <div eID="gen19501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19502" type="x-p"/> His finny coursers, and in triumph rides, <div eID="gen19502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19503" type="x-p"/> The waves unruffle, and the sea subsides. <div eID="gen19503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19504" type="x-p"/> So when the father of the flood appears, <div eID="gen19504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19505" type="x-p"/> And o'er the seas his sovereign trident rears, <div eID="gen19505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19506" type="x-p"/> Their fury fails: he skims the liquid plains <div eID="gen19506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19507" type="x-p"/> High on his chariot; and with loosened reins, <div eID="gen19507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19508" type="x-p"/> Majestic moves along, and awful peace maintains. <div eID="gen19508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19509" type="x-p"/> Dryden. <div eID="gen19509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19510" type="x-p"/> Our God, Jehovah, sitteth upon the flood: yea, Jehovah sitteth King for ever. <div eID="gen19510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19511" type="x-p"/> The heathen god is drawn by his sea-horse, and assisted in his work by subaltern deities: Jehovah sits on the flood an everlasting Governor, ruling all things by his will, maintaining order, and dispensing strength and peace to his people. The description of the Roman poet is fine; that of the Hebrew poet, majestic and sublime.  <chapter eID="Ps.29"/> <div eID="gen19511" type="x-p"/>

entries.b9c246bec3eaa26290c8d9c0a4cf0d20df9437d9: <div eID="gen9348" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">The Psalm of the Seven Thunders</title> <div sID="gen9349" type="x-p"/> The occasion of this Psalm is a thunderstorm; it is not, however, limited to the outward natural phenomena, but therein is perceived the self-attestation of the God of the redemptive history. Just as in the second part of <reference osisRef="Ps.19.1-Ps.19.14">Psa 19:1-14</reference> the God of the revelation of salvation is called יהוה seven times in distinction from the God revealed in nature, so in this Psalm of thunders, קול ה is repeated seven times, so that it may be called the Psalm of the hepta' brontai' (Rev 10:3.). During the time of the second Temple, as the addition to the inscription by the lxx ἐξοδίου (ἐξόδου) σκηνῆς (= σκηνοπηγίας) seems to imply,<note placement="foot">The שׁיר of the Temple liturgy of the <hi type="italic">Shemini Azereth</hi> is not stated in the Talmud (vid., <hi type="italic">Tosefoth</hi> to <hi type="italic">B. Succa</hi> 47 <hi type="italic">a</hi>, where, according to <hi type="italic">Sofrim</hi> xix. §2 and a statement of the Jerusalem Talmud, <reference osisRef="Ps.6.1-Ps.6.10">Psa 6:1-10</reference>, or 12, it guessed at). We only know, that <reference osisRef="Ps.29.1-Ps.29.11">Psa 29:1-11</reference> belongs to the Psalm-portions fore the intervening days of the feast of tabernacles, which are comprehended in the <hi type="italic">vox</hi> <hi type="italic">memorialis</hi> בהיהום (<hi type="italic">Succa</hi> 55 <hi type="italic">a</hi>, cf. Rashi on <hi type="italic">Joma</hi> 3 <hi type="italic">a</hi>), viz., <reference osisRef="Ps.29.1-Ps.29.11">Psa 29:1-11</reference> ()ה; <reference osisRef="Ps.50.16">Psa 50:16</reference> ()ו; <reference osisRef="Ps.94.16">Psa 94:16</reference> ()מ; <reference osisRef="Ps.94.8">Psa 94:8</reference> ()ב; <reference osisRef="Ps.81.7">Psa 81:7</reference> ()ה; <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.82.5">Psa 82:5</reference></hi> ()י. Besides this the treatise <hi type="italic">Sofrim</hi> xviii. §3 mentions <reference osisRef="Ps.29.1-Ps.29.11">Psa 29:1-11</reference> as the Psalm for the festival of Pentecost and the tradition of the synagogue which prevails even at the present day recognises it only as a festival Psalm of the first day of Shabuoth Pentecost; the Psalm for Shemini Azereth is the 65th. The only confirmation of the statement of the lxx is to be found in the Sohar; for there (section )צ <reference osisRef="Ps.29.1-Ps.29.11">Psa 29:1-11</reference> is referred to the pouring forth of the water on the seventh day of the feast of the tabernacles (<hi type="italic">Hosianna rabba</hi>), since it is said, that by means of the seven קולות (corresponding to the seven compassings of the altar) seven of the <hi type="italic">Sephiroth</hi> open the flood-gates of heaven.</note> it was sung on the <hi type="italic">Shemini Azereth</hi>, the last day (ἐξόδιον, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.36">Lev 23:36</reference>) of the feast of tabernacles. Between two tetrastichs, in each of which the name יהוה occurs four times, lie three pentastichs, which, in their sevenfold קול ה, represent the peals of thunder which follow in rapid succession as the storm increases in its fury.
entries.d241638c226ee3e03522beca7e0f71da977c1aca: <reference osisRef="Ps.29.1-Ps.29.2">Psa 29:1-2</reference> <div eID="gen9349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9350" type="x-p"/> The opening strophe calls upon the celestial spirits to praise Jahve; for a revelation of divine glory is in preparation, which, in its first movements, they are accounted worthy to behold, for the roots of everything that takes place in this world are in the invisible world. It is not the mighty of the earth, who are called in <reference osisRef="Ps.82.6">Psa 82:6</reference> בּני עליון, but the angels, who are elsewhere called בּני אלהים (e.g., <reference osisRef="Job.2.1">Job 2:1</reference>), that are here, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.89.7">Psa 89:7</reference>, called בּני אלים. Since אלים never means God, like אלהים (so that it could be rendered sons of the deity), but gods, <reference osisRef="Exod.15.11">Exo 15:11</reference>, Dan. 9:36, the expression בּני אלים must be translated as a double plural from בּן־אל, after the analogy of בּתּי כלאים, <reference osisRef="Isa.42.22">Isa 42:22</reference>, from בּית כּלא (Ges. §108, 3), “sons of God,” not “sons of gods.” They, the God-begotten, i.e., created in the image of God, who form with God their Father as it were one family (vid., <hi type="italic">Genesis</hi> S. 1212), are here called upon to give unto God glory and might (the primary passage is <reference osisRef="Deut.32.3">Deu 32:3</reference>), i.e., to render back to Him cheerfully and joyously in a laudatory recognition, as it were by an echo, His glory and might, which are revealed and to be revealed in the created world, and to give unto Him the glory of His name, i.e., to praise His glorious name (<reference osisRef="Ps.72.19">Psa 72:19</reference>) according its deserts. הבוּ in all three instances has the accent on the <hi type="italic">ultima</hi> according to rule (cf. on the other hand, <reference osisRef="Job.6.22">Job 6:22</reference>). הדרת קדשׁ is holy vestments, splendid festal attire, <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.21">2Ch 20:21</reference>, cf. Psa 110:3.<note placement="foot">The reading proposed in <hi type="italic">B. Berachoth 30b</hi> בּחרדּת (with holy trembling) has never been a various reading; nor has בּחצרת, after which the lxx renders it ἐν αὐλῇ ἁγίᾳ αὐτοῦ.</note> <div eID="gen9350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9351" type="x-p"/> A revelation of the power of God is near at hand. The heavenly spirits are to prepare themselves for it with all the outward display of which they are capable. If <reference osisRef="Ps.28.2">Psa 28:2</reference> were a summons to the church on earth, or, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.96.9">Psa 96:9</reference>, to the dwellers upon the earth, then there ought to be some expression to indicate the change in the parties addressed; it is, therefore, in <reference osisRef="Ps.28.2">Psa 28:2</reference> as in <reference osisRef="Ps.28.1">Psa 28:1</reference>, directed to the priests of the heavenly היכל. In the Apocalypse, also, the songs of praise and trumpeting of the angels precede the judgments of God.
entries.5fb023f4d8184f2be28d3a36990e7dc57717718f: <reference osisRef="Ps.29.3-Ps.29.9">Psa 29:3-9</reference> <div eID="gen9351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9352" type="x-p"/> Now follows the description of the revelation of God’s power, which is the ground of the summons, and is to be the subject-matter of their praise. The All-glorious One makes Himself heard in the language (Rev 10:3.) of the thunder, and reveals Himself in the storm. There are fifteen lines, which naturally arrange themselves into three five-line strophes. The chief matter with the poet, however, is the sevenfold קול ה. Although קול is sometimes used almost as an ejaculatory “Hark!” (<reference osisRef="Gen.4.10">Gen 4:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.52.8">Isa 52:8</reference>), this must not, with Ewald (§286, <hi type="italic">f</hi>), be applied to the קול ה of the Psalm before us, the theme of which is the voice of God, who announced Himself from heaven - a voice which moves the world. The dull sounding קול serves not merely to denote the thunder of the storm, but even the thunder of the earthquake, the roar of the tempest, and in general, every low, dull, rumbling sound, by which God makes Himself audible to the world, and more especially from the wrathful side of His doxa. The waters in <reference osisRef="Ps.29.3">Psa 29:3</reference> are not the lower waters. Then the question arises what are they? Were the waters of the Mediterranean intended, they would be more definitely denoted in such a vivid description. It is, however, far more appropriate to the commencement of this description to understand them to mean the mass of water gathered together in the thick, black storm-clouds (vid., <reference osisRef="Ps.18.12">Psa 18:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.10.13">Jer 10:13</reference>). The rumbling<note placement="foot">The simple rendering of קול by “voice” has been retained in the text of the Psalm, as in the Authorised Version. The word, however, which Dr. Delitzsch uses is <hi type="italic">Gedröhn</hi>, the best English equivalent of which is a “rumbling.” - Tr.</note> of Jahve is, as the poet himself explains in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.29.3">Psa 29:3</reference></hi>, the thunder produced on high by the אל הכּבוד (cf. מלך הכבוד, Psa 24:7.), which rolls over the sea of waters floating above the earth in the sky. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.29.4">Psa 29:4</reference></hi> and <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.29.4">Psa 29:4</reference></hi>, just like <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.29.3">Psa 29:3</reference></hi> and <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.29.3">Psa 29:3</reference></hi>, are independent substantival clauses. The rumbling of Jahve is, issues forth, or passes by; ב with the abstract article as in <reference osisRef="Ps.77.14">Psa 77:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.24.5">Pro 24:5</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.8.8">Pro 8:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.4.32">Luk 4:32</reference>, ἐν ἰσχύΐ <reference osisRef="Rev.18.2">Rev 18:2</reference>), is the ב of the distinctive attribute. In <reference osisRef="Ps.29.3">Psa 29:3</reference> the first peals of thunder are heard; in <reference osisRef="Ps.29.4">Psa 29:4</reference> the storm is coming nearer, and the peals become stronger, and now it bursts forth with its full violence: <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.29.5">Psa 29:5</reference></hi> describes this in a general form, and <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.29.5">Psa 29:5</reference></hi> expresses by the <hi type="italic">fut. consec</hi>., as it were inferentially, that which is at present taking place: amidst the rolling of the thunder the descending lightning flashes rive the cedars of Lebanon (as is well-known, the lightning takes the outermost points). The suffix in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.29.6">Psa 29:6</reference> </hi>does not refer proleptically to the mountains mentioned afterwards, but naturally to the cedars (Hengst., Hupf., Hitz.), which bend down before the storm and quickly rise up again. The skipping of Lebanon and Sirion, however, is not to be referred to the fact, that their wooded summits bend down and rise again, but, according to <reference osisRef="Ps.114.4">Psa 114:4</reference>, to their being shaken by the crash of the thunder-a feature in the picture which certainly does not rest upon what is actually true in nature, but figuratively describes the apparent quaking of the earth during a heavy thunderstorm. שריון, according to <reference osisRef="Deut.3.9">Deu 3:9</reference>, is the Sidonian name of Hermon, and therefore side by side with Lebanon it represents Anti-Lebanon. The word, according to the Masora, has ש <hi type="italic">sinistrum</hi>, and consequently is isriyown, wherefore Hitzig correctly derives it from Arab. <hi type="italic">srâ , fut</hi>. i., to gleam, sparkle, cf. the passage from an Arab poet at Psa 133:3. The lightning makes these mountains bound (Luther, <hi type="italic">lecken</hi>, i.e., according to his explanation: to spring, skip) like young antelopes. ראם,<note placement="foot">On Arab. <hi type="italic">r'm</hi> vid., Seetzen’s <hi type="italic">Reisen</hi> iii. 339 and also iv. 496.</note> like βούβαλος, βούβαλις, is a generic name of the antelope, and of the buffalo that roams in herds through the forests beyond the Jordan even at the present day; for there are antelopes that resemble the buffalo and also (except in the formation of the head and the cloven hoofs) those that resemble the horse, the lxx renders: ὡς υἱὸς μονοκερώτων. Does this mean the unicorn Germ. one-horn depicted on Persian and African monuments? Is this unicorn distinct from the one horned antelope? Neither an unicorn nor an one horned antelope have been seen to the present day by any traveller. Both animals, and consequently also their relation to one another, are up to the present time still undefinable from a scientific point of view.<note placement="foot">By ראם Ludolf in opposition to Bochart understands the rhinoceros; but this animal, belonging to the swine tribe, is certainly not meant, or even merely associated with it. Moreover, the rhinoceros Germ. nose-horn is called in Egypt <hi type="italic">charnin</hi> (from Arab. <hi type="italic">chrn = qrn</hi>), but the unicorn, <hi type="italic">charnit</hi>. “In the year 1862 the French archaeologist, M. Among the well known animals there was also an unicorn, exactly like a zebra or a horse, but with a long horn standing out upon its forehead; on its body was the word Arab. <hi type="italic">chrnı̂t</hi>. M. Waddington wished to have the vessel and I gave it up to him; and he took it with him to Paris. We talked a good deal about this unicorn, and felt obliged to come to the conclusion that the form of the fabulous animal might have become known to the Arabs at the time of the crusades, when the English coat of arms came to Syria.” - Wetzstein.</note> <div eID="gen9352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9353" type="x-p"/> Each peal of thunder is immediately followed by a flash of lightning; Jahve’s thunder cleaveth flames of fire, i.e., forms (as it were λατομεῖ) the fire-matter of the storm-clouds into cloven flames of fire, into lightnings that pass swiftly along; in connection with which it must be remembered that קול ה denotes not merely the thunder as a phenomenon, but at the same time it denotes the omnipotence of God expressing itself therein. The brevity and threefold division of <reference osisRef="Ps.29.7">Psa 29:7</reference> depicts the incessant, zigzag, quivering movement of the lightning (<hi type="italic">tela trisulca, ignes trisulci</hi>, in Ovid). From the northern mountains the storm sweeps on towards the south of Palestine into the Arabian desert, viz., as we are told in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.29.8">Psa 29:8</reference></hi> (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.29.5">Psa 29:5</reference>, according to the schema of “parallelism by reservation”), the wilderness region of <hi type="italic">Kadesh (Kadesh Barnea)</hi>, which, however we may define its position, must certainly have lain near the steep western slope of the mountains of Edom toward the Arabah. Jahve’s thunder, viz., the thunderstorm, puts this desert in a state of whirl, inasmuch as it drives the sand (חול) before it in whirlwinds; and among the mountains it, viz., the strong lightning and thundering, makes the hinds to writhe, inasmuch as from fright they bring forth prematurely. both the <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. יהיל and the <hi type="italic">Pil</hi>. יחולל are used with a causative meaning (root חו, חי, to move in a circle, to encircle). The poet continues with ויּחשׂף, since he makes one effect of the storm to develope from another, merging as it were out of its chrysalis state. יערות is a poetical plural form; and חשׂף describes the effect of the storm which “shells” the woods, inasmuch as it beats down the branches of the trees, both the tops and the foliage. While Jahve thus reveals Himself from heaven upon the earth in all His irresistible power, בּהיכלו, in His heavenly palace (<reference osisRef="Ps.11.4">Psa 11:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.18.7">Psa 18:7</reference>), כּלּו (note how בהיכלו resolves this כלו out of itself), i.e., each of the beings therein, says: כבוד. That which the poet, in <reference osisRef="Ps.29.1">Psa 29:1</reference>, has called upon them to do, now takes place. Jahve receives back His glory, which is immanent in the universe, in the thousand-voiced echo of adoration.
entries.f335de73dcd8f868f3fd071f8fe12d3ab8d958a6: <reference osisRef="Ps.29.10-Ps.29.11">Psa 29:10-11</reference> <div eID="gen9353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9354" type="x-p"/> Luther renders it: “The Lord sitteth to prepare a Flood,” thus putting meaning into the unintelligible rendering of the Vulgate and lxx; and in fact a meaning that accords with the language - for ישׁב ל is most certainly intended to be understood after the analogy of ישׁב למשׁפט, <reference osisRef="Ps.122.5">Psa 122:5</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.9.8">Psa 9:8</reference> - just as much as with the context; for the poet has not thus far expressly referred to the torrents of rain, in which the storm empties itself. Engelhardt also (<hi type="italic">Lutherische Zeitschrift</hi>, 1861, 216f.), Kurtz (<hi type="italic">Bibel und Astronomie</hi>, S. 568, Aufl. 4), Riehm (<hi type="italic">Liter. - Blatt</hi> of the <hi type="italic">Allgem. Kirchen-Zeit.</hi>, 1864, S. 110), and others understand by מבול the quasi-flood of the torrent of rain accompanying the lightning and thunder. But the word is not למבול, but למּבול, and המּבּוּל (Syr. <hi type="italic">momûl</hi>) occurs exclusively in <reference osisRef="Gen.6.11">Gen 6-11</reference> as the name of the great Flood. Every tempest, however, calls to mind this judgment and its merciful issue, for it comes before us in sacred history as the first appearance of rain with lightning and thunder, and of the bow in the clouds speaking its message of peace (<hi type="italic">Genesis</hi>, S. 276). The retrospective reference to this event is also still further confirmed by the aorist ויּשׁב which follows the perfect ישׁב (Hofmann, <hi type="italic">Schriftbeweis</hi> i. 208). Jahve - says the poet - sat (upon His throne) at the Flood (to execute it), and sits (enthroned) in consequence thereof, or since that time, as this present revelation of Him in the tempest shows, as King for ever, inasmuch as He rules down here upon earth from His throne in the heavens (<reference osisRef="Ps.115.16">Psa 115:16</reference>) in wrath and in mercy, judging and dispensing blessing. Here upon earth He has a people, whom from above He endows with a share of His own might and blesses with peace, while the tempests of His wrath burst over their foes. How expressive is בּשּׁלום as the closing word of this particular Psalm! It spans the Psalm like a rain-bow. The opening of the Psalm shows us the heavens opened and the throne of God in the midst of the angelic songs of praise, and the close of the Psalm shows us, on earth, His people victorious and blessed with peace (בּ as in <reference osisRef="Gen.24.1">Gen 24:1</reference> <note placement="foot">The Holy One, blessed be He-says the Mishna, <hi type="italic">Uksin</hi> iii. 12, with reference to this passage in the Psalms-has not found any other vessel (כלי) to hold the blessing specially allotted to Israel but peace.)</note> in the midst of Jahve’s voice of anger, which shakes all things. <hi type="italic">Gloria in excelsis</hi> is its beginning, and <hi type="italic">pax in terris</hi> its conclusion.  <chapter eID="Ps.29"/> <div eID="gen9354" type="x-p"/>

PSALM 29.
David, that he may humble all men before God, from the highest to the lowest, celebrates his terrible power in the various wonders of nature, which he affirms are not less fitted to arouse us to give glory to God, than if he were to assert his empire and majesty with his own voice. After he has struck fear into the proud, who are reluctant to yield, and addressed an exhortation to them accompanied by a gentle reproof, he sweetly invites the faithful voluntarily to fear the Lord.
A Psalm of David.
Psalm 29:1-4
1. Give unto Jehovah, ye sons of the mighty, give unto Jehovah glory and strength. 2. Give unto Jehovah the glory of his name;
“C’est, digne de son nom.” — Note, Fr. Marg. “That is, worthy of his name.”
worship before Jehovah in the brightness of his sanctuary. 3. The voice of Jehovah is upon the waters; the God of glory thundereth; Jehovah is upon the great waters. 4. The voice of Jehovah is in strength, the voice of Jehovah is in beauty.
 
1. Give unto Jehovah, ye sons of the mighty. It was no doubt David’s design to lead all men to worship and reverence God; but as it is more difficult to reduce great men, who excel in rank, to order, he expressly addresses himself to them. It is obvious, that the LXX, in giving the translation, sons of rams,
The entire reading of the verse in the Septuagint is, “Ενέγκατε τῷ Κυρίῳ ὑιοὶ Θεοῦ ενέγκατε τῷ Κυρίῳ ὑιοὺς κριῶν” “Bring to the Lord, ye sons of God, bring to the Lord young rams.” Thus the LXX, as is not unusual in other places, render the words for “Ye sons of the mighty” twice; first, in the vocative case, addressing them, Υιοὶ Θεου, Ye sons of God, and then in the accusative case, ὑιοὺς κριῶν, young rams, being apparently doubtful which was the correct rendering, and, therefore, putting down both. The Vulgate, Arabic, and Ethiopic, exactly follow them. Jerome also reads, “Afferte Domino filios arietum;” although he does not give a double translation of the original words. But the correct rendering, we have no doubt, is, “Ye sons of the mighty;” which is just a Hebrew idiomatic expression for “Ye mighty ones,” or, “Ye princes;” and to them the inspired writer addresses an invitation to acknowledge and worship God from the manifestation of his majesty and power in the wonders of nature.
were led into a mistake by the affinity of the Hebrew words.
The Hebrew word which Calvin renders “mighty,” is אלים, elym, a word which means gods. The Hebrew word אילים, eylim, which means rams, nearly resembles it, having only an additional י, yod, and this letter is often cut off in nouns.
About the signification of the word, indeed, the Jewish commentators are all agreed; but when they proceed to speak of its meaning, they pervert and obscure it by the most chilling comments. Some expound it of the angels,
The Chaldee paraphrases it thus:— “The assembly of angels, sons of God,” meaning by God angels.
some of the stars; and others will have it, that by the great men who are referred to are meant the holy fathers. But David only intended to humble the princes of this world, who, being intoxicated with pride, lift up their horns against God. This, accordingly, is the reason why he introduces God, with a terrific voice, subduing by thunders, hail-storms, tempests, and lightnings, these stubborn and stiff-necked giants, who, if they are not struck with fear, refuse to stand in awe of any power in heaven. We see, therefore, why, passing by others, he directs his discourse particularly to the sons of the mighty. The reason is, because there is nothing more common with them than to abuse their lofty station by impious deeds, while they madly arrogate to themselves every divine prerogative. At least that they may modestly submit themselves to God, and, mindful of their frailty, place their dependence upon his grace, it is necessary, as it were, to compel them by force. David, therefore, commands them to give strength unto Jehovah, because, deluded by their treacherous imaginations, they think that the power which they possess is supplied to them from some other quarter than from heaven. In short, he exhorts them to lay aside their haughtiness, and their false opinion about their own strength, and to glorify God as he deserves. By the glory of God’s name, (ver. 2,) he means that which is worthy of his majesty, of which the great men of this world are wont to deprive him. The repetition, also, shows that they must be vehemently urged ere a proper acknowledgement be extorted from them. By the brightness of God’s sanctuary
This translation conveys a somewhat different meaning from that of our English version; but it is supported by several critics. Green reads, “In his beautiful sanctuary;” and Fry, “Worship Jehovah with holy reverence,” or, “Worship Jehovah in the glorious places of the sanctuary.” “Where the Hebrews read בהדרת” says Hammond, “in the glory or beauty of holiness, from הדר, to honor, or beautify, the LXX. read, ἐν αὐλὣ ἁγίᾳ αὐτου, in his holy court, as if it were from, “penetrale, thalamus, area, a closet, a marriage-chamber, a court; and so the Latin and Syriac follow them, and the Arabic, in his “holy habitation.”
is to be understood, not heaven as some think, but the tabernacle of the covenant, adorned with the symbols of the divine glory, as is evident from the context. And the prophet designedly makes mention of this place, in which the true God had manifested himself, that all men, bidding adieu to superstition, should betake themselves to the pure worship of God. It would not be sufficient to worship any heavenly power, but the one and unchangeable God alone must be worshipped, which cannot come to pass until the world be reclaimed from all foolish inventions and services forged in the brains of men.
